title: Where the Optical Interposer fits in the CPO landscape
body:
## The Architectural Fork

The datacenter optical interconnect market is, at its core, a dispute about where to put the light. For two decades, the answer was settled: a pluggable transceiver module, slotting into a cage on the faceplate of a switch or server, converting electrical signals from the ASIC to photons on the fibre. It was a clean, modular, serviceably competitive market. Then the AI training cluster arrived and began consuming bandwidth at rates that made the pluggable paradigm's power budget and signal-integrity losses look like a structural tax on compute density.

Co-packaged optics — moving the optical engine from the faceplate into the switch package itself, integrating it directly with the switch ASIC — was not a new concept when hyperscalers began entertaining it seriously in 2022 and 2023. What changed was the economic pressure: 800G and 1.6T link speeds demand that the electrical signal path between the ASIC serialiser and the optical modulator be measured in millimetres, not centimetres. At 1.6T, the electrical loss on a pluggable-length trace erases margin that simply does not exist. The industry's architectural debate hardened from theoretical to urgent.

POET Technologies, incorporated in Toronto with its wafer-level fabrication operations housed at POET Singapore Pte. Ltd., staked its entire commercial thesis on the CPO transition occurring at scale. The company's FY2025 annual report, filed as a 20-F with the SEC, disclosed approximately $1.2 million of non-recurring engineering and small-product revenue against a $62.96 million net loss — numbers that make POET's financial profile unambiguously pre-commercial. The investment question is not about quarterly execution. It is about architectural outcome.

## How the Optical Interposer Differs from the Field

The CPO competitive landscape stratified, by 2025, into four structurally distinct approaches — and understanding POET's position requires holding all four simultaneously.

The first and dominant strand is **integrated silicon photonics**. Intel Photonics operates a silicon-only photonic integration line, internally deployed; Marvell absorbed Inphi's coherent DSP capability and has layered optical-engine assets atop it; Cisco acquired Acacia; Coherent built a vertically integrated compound-semiconductor and silicon photonics platform. These players share a common constraint: their integration approach is defined by the underlying process technology. Silicon photonics provides excellent passive components and acceptable modulators, but silicon emits no light efficiently at telecom wavelengths, requiring external or attached laser sources — a problem solved in various ways by each player, none elegantly.

The second strand is **compound-semiconductor monolithic integration** — historical InP platforms that attempt to grow lasers, modulators, and photodetectors on a single wafer of indium phosphide. High-performance, high-cost, difficult to yield at wafer scale.

The third strand is **chip-to-chip optical I/O** — Ayar Labs, Lightmatter, and Celestial AI each approached the problem from the compute-die side rather than the switch-ASIC side, designing photonic chiplets intended to replace copper die-to-die interconnect inside a package. This is a structurally different addressable market: it targets memory bandwidth and AI-accelerator die disaggregation, not the hyperscaler fabric switch.

POET's Optical Interposer falls into a fourth category: **materials-agnostic wafer-level photonic integration on a passive substrate**. The architecture is explicitly not tied to silicon as the base process. Multiple classes of active components — InP lasers, modulators, photodetectors, passive silicon filters — can be assembled onto the interposer substrate with heterogeneous integration, combining the best emitter performance from compound semiconductors with silicon's passive-optical precision. The passive substrate approach minimises optical coupling loss at each interface, which is the dominant yield-killer in heterogeneous photonic assembly. Whether POET's specific implementation of this architecture at production volumes can match the cost curve of silicon photonics incumbents remained unresolved at the snapshot date.

## The Competitive Map at a Glance

| Player | Approach | CPO Role | Revenue Scale | Key Asset |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Intel Photonics | Silicon-only integrated PIC | Optical engine supplier (internal) | Large (embedded in Intel segments) | Internal foundry, co-design with Ethernet switch |
| Marvell (Inphi) | PAM-DSP + silicon photonics optical engines | DSP and optical engine supplier | Large ($1B+ optics segment) | Inphi DSP IP, hyperscaler design wins |
| Coherent (II-VI) | Vertically integrated InP + SiPh | Transceiver, optical engine, ELS | Large ($4B+ revenue) | Vertical integration, ELS laser IP |
| Lumentum | DFB lasers, pluggable modules | Laser source supplier; pluggable incumbent | Mid ($1.5B+ revenue) | Laser yield, pluggable volume relationships |
| Broadcom (Tomahawk CPO) | Switch ASIC with integrated CPO | Switch ASIC *and* CPO platform definer | Very large ($30B+ revenue) | Tomahawk market share, hyperscaler socket |
| Ayar Labs | Intra-chip optical I/O | AI-accelerator chiplet | Pre-revenue (venture) | TSMC integration, memory-bandwidth thesis |
| Lightmatter | Photonic interconnect interposer | AI-cluster fabric (different problem) | Pre-revenue (venture) | Significant venture funding 2024–2025 |
| **POET Technologies** | **Materials-agnostic optical interposer** | **ELS module + transceiver component** | **Pre-revenue (~$1.2M NRE FY25)** | **Heterogeneous integration IP, $313M cash** |

The table above understates the asymmetry: every named incumbent except Ayar, Lightmatter, and Celestial AI was generating hundreds of millions to billions of dollars of annual revenue at the snapshot date. POET was generating $341,000 in its strongest quarter of FY2025. The question for POET shareholders is not whether the company is better capitalised than a silicon photonics startup — the $250 million institutional equity raise, completed in 2025 and leaving $313.4 million in cash and short-term investments on the FY2025 balance sheet, resolved that question. The question is whether materials-agnostic interposer integration is structurally differentiated enough to win qualified positions in hyperscaler CPO supply chains before silicon photonics incumbents lock out non-silicon approaches at the architectural level.

## The Sivers Partnership and the ELS Use Case

The most concretely disclosed partner relationship at the snapshot date was the September 2025 collaboration with Sivers Semiconductors, specifically Sivers Photonics, the Swedish company's UK-based III-V laser subsidiary. [POET Technologies / Sivers collaboration press release](https://www.poet-technologies.com/news/poet-technologies-and-sivers-semiconductors-collaborate-on-external-light-sources-for-co-packaged-optics-and-next-generation-ai-market) described the arrangement as a combination of Sivers' high-power InP distributed-feedback lasers with POET's Optical Interposer for the external light source module market.

The external light source architecture deserves a precise definition in this context. Pure CPO — where the laser dies inside the package with the switch ASIC — creates a thermal management problem at 800G and beyond. The laser is a heat source attached to a package whose thermal budget is already strained by the switch ASIC's power dissipation. An alternative that has attracted serious hyperscaler engineering attention is the ELS module: a separately housed unit containing the laser array, integrated on an optical interposer, delivering light into the co-packaged optical engine via a fibre or waveguide interface. The laser is still inside the rack, eliminating the electrical-loss penalty of a pluggable module, while the thermal architecture decouples laser cooling from ASIC cooling.

This is POET's most credible near-term wedge. The Sivers collaboration locks in a laser supplier with InP DFB competence. POET's interposer provides the substrate for assembling the laser array, beam-combining optics, and fibre-coupling interface into a manufacturable ELS unit. Neither company had disclosed volume design wins with a named hyperscaler at the snapshot date, but the combination addressed a real and growing problem in CPO system architecture.

## The Broadcom Demand Signal

No single commercial development in the CPO landscape carried more analytical weight in 2025 than Broadcom's Tomahawk 5 CPO programme. Broadcom — the dominant merchant silicon supplier for hyperscaler Ethernet switching — disclosed a co-packaged optical variant of the Tomahawk 5 ASIC intended for production deployment. If Tomahawk 5 CPO reaches volume deployment with major hyperscalers, it represents the clearest possible demand-side validation that the CPO architectural transition is not an engineering-conference aspiration but an operational procurement decision.

The downstream implication for POET is indirect but structural. Broadcom does not publicly disclose its optical-engine supplier list for Tomahawk CPO. But a qualified optical-engine or ELS supplier in the Tomahawk 5 CPO supply chain would have secured the most credible early-volume position in the market. POET's 20-F filing described a customer qualification pattern — engaging through hyperscaler engineering teams and OEM/ODM channels — but disclosed no Tomahawk-programme design win at the snapshot date. Nvidia's Rubin generation CPO disclosures, if they materialised, represented the second major demand-signal the market was tracking: Nvidia's internal silicon photonics roadmap and any CPO commitment at Rubin scale would multiply the addressable market for interposer-based optical engines by adding GPU-to-switch links to the already-large switch-fabric opportunity.

## Structural Position: The Platform Bet with Real Cash

POET's competitive position, assessed against the snapshot date, resolved into a set of durable structural characteristics that distinguished it from both the large-cap incumbents and the venture-funded competitors.

Against Coherent, Lumentum, and Marvell, POET had zero revenue and a research-and-development budget of $18.08 million in FY2025 — a fraction of what any of those companies spent on photonics engineering annually. The materials-agnostic interposer architecture, however sophisticated, would need to clear a qualification bar set by organisations whose photonics teams dwarfed POET's entire headcount. That gap did not make the platform thesis wrong. It did mean the thesis depended on the interposer approach being differentiated enough at the system level that hyperscaler CPO architects sought it out rather than defaulting to captive or incumbent-supplied silicon photonics.

Against Ayar Labs, Lightmatter, and Celestial AI, POET's $313.4 million cash position was a structural advantage of the first order. Venture-backed competitors were navigating a markedly more difficult funding environment in 2025 than in 2021-2022. POET, having secured three institutional buyers in its $250 million equity raise, had bought itself approximately five to seven years of runway at FY2025 burn rates — enough time for the hyperscaler CPO qualification cycle, typically eighteen to thirty-six months from engagement through volume, to run its course twice over.

The board composition carried its own signal. Jean-Louis Malinge, lead independent director, had previously built and sold Kotura — a silicon photonics company — to Mellanox for $82 million, establishing that he had navigated a silicon photonics platform from development through acquisition by a network-silicon incumbent. The analogy was imperfect: Kotura's addressable market and POET's are structurally different, and Mellanox was acquired by Nvidia in 2020 at a radically different valuation. But the precedent established that at least one board member had operated inside the precise intersection of photonics IP and network-silicon M&A that POET's platform thesis ultimately depended on for its exit scenarios.

The honest competitive summary, as of the snapshot date: POET occupied a structurally defensible architectural niche — materials-agnostic heterogeneous photonic integration — at a moment when the CPO transition was moving from engineering prototype to procurement conversation among hyperscalers. The company was capitalised to survive the transition. Whether it would be qualified to benefit from it remained the open question on which the entire investment thesis rested.
